newsitem.title: USA: Jobless rate rises to 5.4 percent, but hiring brisk.
newsitem.headline: Jobless rate rises to 5.4 percent, but hiring brisk.

text.p: The government's first reading of the nation's economic health in January had good news for both workers and financial markets by showing brisk hiring that did not appear to pose an inflationary threat.

The Labour Department said Friday that, despite a statiscially insignificant rise in the unemployment rate to 5.4 percent, the job market was fairly strong last month while wages were almost stagnant.
"It was the best of both worlds," said economist David Jones of Aubrey G. Lanston Co. in New York. "It looks like we're leading a charmed economic life."

The department reported that 271,000 non-farm jobs were created last month, the most since August, after payrolls grew by 261,000 jobs in December. In the past 12 months the economy has created nearly 3 million jobs.

Even though last month's job growth was slightly greater than expected -- a sign of labour market tightness that often worries traders -- stock and bond markets rallied as investors found no signs of the kind of wage-driven inflation that could prompt Federal Reserve policymakers to raise interest rates.

Average hourly wages rose only 1 cent last month to $12.06, after gaining 15 cents in the previous two months, the department said. Over the past 12 months they rose by 3.8 percent, slightly faster than 3.3 percent rise in consumer prices in 1996.
The department's more comprehensive Employment Cost Index, however, rose only 2.9 percent in 1996.

With the economy about to complete its sixth year of uninterrupted growth and the jobless rate at less than 6 percent for almost 2-1/2 years, economists have said some pickup in inflation is likely to come eventually.

While wage gains have accelerated over the past few years, they have been modest because of job insecurity and the impact on inflation has been slight since businesses are reluctant to raise prices in the face of global competition, Jones said.
"That, in turn, has kept the inflation environment remarkably good," he added.

The rise in the January jobless rate to 5.4 percent from 5.3 percent in December was accompanied by a revision in the population estimate used by the department, which caused most of the increase in the civilian labour force of workers and job seekers of about a half-million to 135.8 million.
The department's household survey last month showed a rise of 75,000 unemployed workers to 7.27 million and a gain of 433,000 job holders to 128.58 million.

The vast majority of January's new jobs, 239,000, were in service-producing industries, reflected by stronger gains in health care and transportation jobs, according to the department's survey of payrolls.
However, the department noted slower growth in retail, business service and government jobs.
One of the largest gains was a jump of 82,000 temporary service jobs, leading some economists to question just how much strength there was in the job market last month.
"If you intend to keep the workers around, you don't usually bring in temps," said economist David Wyss of DRI/McGraw-Hill in Lexington, Mass. "Also they don't usually work as many hours."

A rebound in manufacturing employment continued last month as 18,000 workers were added to payrolls. In the past four months factory payrolls have grown by 53,000, after a having shrunk by 319,000 in the 18 months through last September.
The department said harsh winter weather in January reduced total hours worked per week, a key indicator used by some Fed officials in assessing labour market conditions.
The manufacturing work week fell by 18 minutes to 41.7 hours, while factory overtime was unchanged at 4.6 hours per week, the department said.
"If you adjust for the effect of weather, I think basically the outlook is that things are remaining reasonably healthy but not very strong," said Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis.
Nasty weather also slowed growth in construction jobs, the department said. The industry added 14,000 jobs last month after a 55,000 gain in the previous two months.

Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labour Statistics, said a number of statistical quirks may have overstated or understated the number of jobs in specific industries last month, but their net effect on the overall job market should be small.
